facts.statement: An option contract grants the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying asset at a predetermined strike price on or before a specified expiration date, in exchange for an upfront non-refundable option premium.

The four foundational option positions comprise: Long Call (right to buy, limited loss / unlimited gain), Short Call (obligation to sell, capped premium / unlimited loss), Long Put (right to sell, limited loss / substantial gain), and Short Put (obligation to buy, capped premium / substantial downside risk).
American options can be exercised at any point up to expiration. European options can only be exercised on the expiration date itself. Almost all US exchange-traded equity options are American style.
Moneyness: Call options are in-the-money (ITM) when S > K, at-the-money (ATM) when S = K, and out-of-the-money (OTM) when S < K. Puts are ITM when S < K and OTM when S > K.

Stock Split Option Adjustment: For an N-for-M split, the post-split strike K' = K * (M / N), and the number of shares covered by the contract increases to 100 * (N / M). Total contract value (Strike * Shares) remains invariant.

For a 3-for-1 stock split on a contract with strike $150 covering 100 shares: New Strike K' = 150 * (1/3) = $50, and shares per contract become 100 * 3 = 300 shares. Total strike value = $50 * 300 = $15,000, identical to pre-split $150 * 100.

Exchange-traded options are unprotected against ordinary cash dividends. Stock price drops by the dividend amount on the ex-dividend date, benefiting put holders and hurting call holders without contractual adjustment.

In 2004, Gucci paid a massive extraordinary dividend of 13.50 EUR. Under exchange rules, extraordinary dividends exceeding a specific threshold (e.g. 10% of stock price) trigger strike reductions to protect option holders.
